title: Water temperature gave no repeated linear decrease in dam-to-dam conversion of PIT-tagged adult salmon in the Columbia Basin in 2004-2025; lower conversion at 22 C or more came mostly from 2015
abstract: Question: does warm river water during the upstream migration decrease the probability that a PIT-tagged adult salmon reaches the next dam? We used 153,308 fish-reach records (86,813 fish-years) from Columbia River DART for seven stock groups (upper Columbia and Snake sockeye, spring, summer and fall Chinook) in three reaches, 2004-2025. We joined each fish to the mean dam water temperature in its passage window. The planned main model compared fish of the same stock, reach and year, with a common seasonal curve, and used year-bootstrap intervals. We wrote the plan before the fits and tested 2004-2014 and 2015-2025 separately. The pooled change in log odds of conversion per +1 C was +0.039 (95% CI -0.022 to +0.110) in 2004-2014 and -0.092 (-0.230 to +0.108) in 2015-2025. Only 7 of 14 stock-reach slopes had the same sign in both periods. A model fitted on 2004-2014 predicted 2015-2025 outcomes slightly worse with temperature than without it (skill -0.005, CI -0.011 to -0.000). In pooled bin models, fish at 22 C or more had log odds of conversion 0.99 lower than fish at 16-18 C in 2015-2025 (CI -1.36 to -0.13). Without 2015 this contrast was -0.29, so it depends mostly on one year. Converted fish moved faster in warmer water (log travel time -0.051 and -0.076 per C; 13 of 14 series negative), except Snake fall Chinook in the lower river, which moved more slowly. Limitations: year effects leave only 0.2-0.6 C of temperature variation; conversion includes harvest, straying and detection loss as well as death; most tagged fish are hatchery fish; one river basin; correlational design.
